source_title: Difficult negotiations lie ahead in Israel after Netanyahu's bloc lost its parliamentary majority - The Hindu
source_excerpt: Jerusalem Israel's final election results confirmed that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc lost its parliamentary majority and that weeks of difficult negotiations among very different parties, from ultra-Orthodox Jewish to secular to Arab-led, lie ahead. Netanyahu's party claims Israel election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority Netanyahu's party claims Israel election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority Israeli media reported that members of Mr. Netanyahu's party were accusing Qatar — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group Netanyahu's party claims Israel election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority storyline 1 The results released early Friday (October 30, 2026) showed Mr. Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday's (October 27, 2026) election. The main Opposition bloc won 48. Arab-led parties secured the other 19, a historic showing. Now parties must meet, bargain and seek a way to team up for at least 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Mr. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving Prime Minister, remains in charge. “Now comes the truly hard part,” centrist politician Yair Lapid said on X, urging patience and adding, “If you want to know if something's happening behind the silence you're hearing now, the answer is yes.” The President will task someone with forming a government Difficult decisions lie ahead. Will the main Opposition parties that campaigned hard to unseat the divisive Mr. Netanyahu make the politically sensitive choice to partner with Arab-led ones? Or will they toss their vows aside to team up with Mr. Netanyahu in a potentially fractious unity government? Israel piles pressure on Arab parties as Netanyahu seeks government Israel piles pressure on Arab parties as Netanyahu seeks government Israeli President Isaac Herzog called for an investigation into allegations of fraud but cautioned against stigmatising the entire Arab Israeli community, who voted at unprecedented rates Israel piles pressure on Arab parties as Netanyahu seeks government storyline 1 Friday (October 30, 2026) is when much of Israel starts winding down for Shabbat, and it was not clear who might be meeting with whom. Israelis debated possible coalitions and challenges, as some expressed traditional wariness around Arab parties and others insisted it was time for Israel to take a deep breath and embrace them. “There are options for all of this, not like in the United States, where there are only two parties,” said Beny Engalrd, a resident of Tel Aviv. The election results still need to be certified and submitted to the President next Wednesday (November 4, 2026). Then President Isaac Herzog will task someone with forming the new government. That could be the leader of the party that received the most votes — Mr. Netanyahu — or whoever the leaders of the various parties believe is best suited. If multiple attempts to form a government fail, Israel faces a new election early next year. Mr. Herzog this week said he will do everything in his power to avoid that scenario. Netanyahu, Likud target Arab parties without evidence In the hours before final results were announced, Mr. Netanyahu and his Likud party amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance. The Opposition quickly accused Mr. Netanyahu of demonising the Arab population, which makes up 20% of the population and showed up at the polls like never before in outrage over Mr. Netanyahu's far-right allies like National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. His party lost seats. Israel election 2026: Benjamin Netanyahu is down but not out Israel election 2026: Benjamin Netanyahu is down but not out Israel’s tight election leaves Benjamin Netanyahu with a fractured majority and a possible caretaker role amid a three-bloc divide and looming coalition uncertainties Analysis Israel election 2026: Benjamin Netanyahu is down but not out storyline 1 In Mr. Netanyahu's first public comment on Friday (October 30, 2026), he posted on X asserting it is forbidden to form a coalition with Arab parties. The head of Israel's election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, had said “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought before him. In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Mr. Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims but asked the agency to investigate. Israeli media reported that members of Mr. Netanyahu's party were accusing Qatar of involvement — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group. Qatar issued a denial, calling the allegations “ridiculous and dangerous.” As it announced results, the election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. Acting Director General Dean Livne did not elaborate but warned that reports about the investigation had been “entirely unfounded.” “It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the President, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population,” he said. By casting doubt on the vote, Mr. Netanyahu appeared to be trying to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab-led parties. Mr. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for chief rival Gadi Eisenkot or others to join with them. The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to “cast aspersions” on an entire section of the population that “exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner.” The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament, saying that “allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless.” The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week. Once it convenes, Mr. Eisenkot's bloc could join forces with the Arab parties to elect a new Knesset speaker, giving them control over the parliamentary agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed. Already, hundreds of Israelis have been holding rallies urging Mr. Eisenkot and others to join forces with the Arab-led parties, a step that has happened only once before, briefly, in 2021. If Mr. Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be taken to account over years-long corruption allegations, and an inquiry almost certainly would begin into security failures before the devastating Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack.
